summary: The whole initiative is one missing concept: the shipping path has no notion of a PERMANENT failure. `createHttpTransport` flattens 401/400/413/503/network into one untyped Error (transport.ts:21), `doShip` treats them identically (retain the whole store, back off to a 30-minute ceiling, log locally), and the Worker turns any D1/R2 fault into a bare runtime 500 with no body — which the client then also reads as 'retry forever'. The smallest design that fully retires both findings is therefore: (1) make the Worker's own faults legible and retryable-by-contract (503 JSON) so a storage outage is honestly transient, (2) give the transport a typed rejection carrying `status` and a `retryable` verdict, (3) let the queue act on that verdict — retryable keeps today's exact retain-and-backoff, auth-permanent enters a `blocked` state that genuinely stops the wakeup treadmill (gated at doShip AND at enqueue, not merely at the reschedule site), other-permanent dead-letters the shipped batch to `<path>.deadletter.jsonl` so one poison item can never block the items behind it, and (4) cut batches by byte budget so the report queue (2MB cap) can never post a body the Worker rejects at its 1MB cap in the first place. The queue's isolation invariant is deliberately preserved: it still never emits onto the Monitor bus. It exposes `state()` plus two injected callbacks — `onStateChange` (fires ONLY on a state transition) and `onDeadLetter` (fires on EVERY dead-lettered batch, because a dead-letter is an event, not a state) — and the composition root (main.ts), not the queue, turns those into Monitor `system` events, so a shipping failure still cannot recurse into the stream it ships. Rejected alternatives: retry-classification inside the Worker (wrong side of the trust boundary), a bespoke backups-health UI panel (buys a design-system + ui-shot pass for signal the Monitor already carries), and a full outbox rewrite (the existing queue is a deep, well-tested module — this adds a policy branch, not a new mechanism).

design.title: Worker fault boundary: storage faults become 503 JSON, size cap becomes byte-accurate and pre-buffer
design.intent: The Worker is the thing you rely on when everything else is broken, so it must fail legibly. Extract the routing body of `default.fetch` in workers/error-ingest/src/index.ts into an internal `async function route(req, env): Promise<Response>` (NOT exported — the module's public surface stays `default.fetch`), and have `fetch` call it inside a try/catch that logs via `console.error('[ingest] route fault', err)` and returns `json({ status: 503, body: { error: 'storage unavailable', detail: err instanceof Error ? err.message : String(err) } })`. Any D1 rate-limit, post-migration schema mismatch, or R2 outage from d1Store/r2Store now becomes a structured, explicitly-retryable response instead of a bare runtime 500. Separately, fix the two size caps: before `await req.text()` on both POST routes, read `req.headers.get('content-length')` and reject 413 immediately when it parses to a finite number above the limit (fast reject, no buffering); after reading, replace `raw.length` (UTF-16 code units, up to 3x under-counting a non-ASCII stack trace) with `new TextEncoder().encode(raw).byteLength` as the authoritative check — content-length is client-supplied and cannot be the only gate. Both checks share one helper `function tooLarge(raw: string, max: number): boolean` plus `function declaredTooLarge(req: Request, max: number): boolean`. MAX_BODY_BYTES (1_000_000) and MAX_BACKUP_BODY_BYTES (16_000_000) are unchanged. Note the surface the implementer may rely on: `fetch` reads exactly `req.url`, `req.method`, `req.headers` and `req.text()` — nothing else — which is what makes the fake-Request verification below executable. Update workers/error-ingest/README.md's response table with the 503 row and the byte-accurate cap.
design.verification: New cases in workers/error-ingest/test/index.test.ts: (a) 'returns 503 JSON when D1 faults' — Env whose `DB.prepare` throws, POST /ingest with a valid single-report batch, assert `res.status === 503` and `(await res.json()).error === 'storage unavailable'`; (b) 'returns 503 JSON when R2 faults' — same via `BACKUPS.put` throwing on POST /backups; (c) 'rejects an oversized declared content-length WITHOUT reading the body' — REPAIRED per fable attack 3, whose objection is correct: a `DB.prepare` spy is vacuously un-called on today's 413 path too (index.ts:40-41 rejects before ingestBatch, and DB access at :54-63 is already unreachable), so it proves nothing about buffering. Instead spy on body consumption directly: build a Request-like object `{ method: 'POST', url: 'https://w/ingest', headers: new Headers({ authorization: 'Bearer secret', 'content-length': '99999999' }), text: vi.fn(async () => '{}') } as unknown as Request` (legal because S1's intent pins the four members `fetch` touches), pass it to `worker.fetch`, and assert `res.status === 413` AND `textSpy` was never called — an implementation that buffers first and checks after fails this, which is the property the step exists to create; (d) 'counts bytes not code units' — a body of 400_000 emoji (1.6MB UTF-8, 800k UTF-16 units) with NO content-length header against MAX_BODY_BYTES, assert 413 where today it passes. Run `pnpm --filter @ledrums/error-ingest-worker test` and `pnpm --filter @ledrums/error-ingest-worker typecheck`; the existing 4 auth/404/400 cases in that file must stay green unchanged.
design.reverses: Single-file revert of index.ts; the extracted `route` is internal so nothing outside the module binds to it. The Worker is deployed separately (`pnpm --filter @ledrums/error-ingest-worker deploy`) — rolling back code alone is not enough, the previous version must be redeployed.

design.title: Typed transport rejection: ShipHttpError with status + retryable verdict
design.intent: Stop discarding the status class at apps/server/src/telemetry/transport.ts:21. Add `export class ShipHttpError extends Error { readonly status: number; readonly retryable: boolean; constructor(status: number) }` with `name = 'ShipHttpError'`, message kept byte-identical to today (`ingest responded ${status}`) so existing assertions and log lines do not change. Classification lives in one exported predicate `export function isRetryableStatus(status: number): boolean` — true for status >= 500, 408, 429; false otherwise. `createHttpTransport` throws `new ShipHttpError(res.status)` instead of a bare Error. A rejected `doFetch` (DNS failure, offline, TLS) is left untouched and propagates as whatever it already is — an unclassified rejection, which the queue will keep treating as retryable. This step is deliberately behaviour-neutral at the queue: `doShip` still catches everything identically, so it lands as its own green commit and the classification can be reviewed in isolation. Deploy-skew note (fable attack 6, which SURVIVED the plan's answer): a pre-S1 Worker's bare runtime 500 classifies retryable, i.e. exactly today's behaviour, so S2-S5 are safe against either live Worker version in either order.
design.verification: Extend apps/server/src/telemetry/transport.test.ts: the existing 'throws on a non-2xx' case keeps asserting `.rejects.toThrow('429')` AND now additionally asserts `instanceof ShipHttpError`, `.status === 429`, `.retryable === true`; new cases assert 401 → retryable false / status 401, 400 → retryable false, 503 → retryable true, 413 → retryable false. Unit-test `isRetryableStatus` at the 4xx/5xx boundary (499 false, 500 true, 408 true, 429 true). Run `pnpm --filter @ledrums/server test -- transport` then `pnpm gates`.

design.title: ShipQueue outcome policy: a blocked state that truly stops shipping, plus dead-letter for poison batches
design.intent:
Make the queue act on the verdict S2 produces — this is the step that retires the 'wedged forever at the 30-minute ceiling' hole. In apps/server/src/telemetry/ship-queue.ts, add internal `let blocked = false` and `let lastState: 'ok' | 'retrying' | 'blocked' = 'ok'`, plus one internal helper `function setState(next, detail)` that assigns `lastState` and calls `opts.onStateChange?.(next, detail)` ONLY when `next !== lastState`. Replace the single catch in `doShip` with a three-way branch on the rejection: (1) unclassified rejection, or `ShipHttpError` with `retryable === true` → EXACTLY today's path (failures++, log, retain the batch, caller reschedules with backoff) plus one added line `setState('retrying', ...)` — this is the parity anchor and the added line is invisible to every existing test because none injects `onStateChange`; (2) `ShipHttpError` with status 401 or 403 → set `blocked = true`, log, retain the batch, do NOT increment failures, and `setState('blocked', \`ingest rejected credentials (${status})\`)`; (3) any other `ShipHttpError` with `retryable === false` (400/404/413/422/…) → append the shipped batch, one JSON item per line, to `${opts.path}.deadletter.jsonl`, remove exactly those keys from `store`/`lengths` (same removal loop as the success path, minus the dropped-counter reset), set `failures = 0`, log the status and item count, call `opts.onDeadLetter?.(batch.length, status)`, and then `setState('ok', ...)`. The queue keeps draining, so one poison item can never block the items behind it.

BLOCKED IS ENFORCED AT THREE SITES, not one (REPAIRED per fable attack 1, which is correct and material: gating only the reschedule site leaves `enqueue`'s unconditional `scheduleFlush(flushIntervalMs)` at ship-queue.ts:206 re-arming the timer on every upsert from a live error stream, so a 'blocked' queue would still POST one rejected request per flush interval forever). (i) `doShip` takes a private parameter `doShip(force = false)` and returns `Promise.resolve()` immediately when `blocked && !force` — this is the authoritative guard, so no path can ship while blocked; (ii) `enqueue` skips `scheduleFlush` while `blocked` (it still keys, sizes, `enforceCaps()` and `schedulePersist()`, so nothing about retention or durability changes); (iii) `tick` and `flush`'s trailing reschedule skip `scheduleFlush` while `blocked`, so no timer survives the transition. `flush()` is the operator escape hatch: it clears `blocked = false` and calls `doShip(true)`, so a re-baked token recovers without a restart.

THE STATE-CHANGE CONTRACT IS EXPLICIT AND HAS A PRODUCER FOR EVERY LABEL (REPAIRED per fable attack 2, which is correct: the original text said 'transitions only' while also emitting `onStateChange('ok', 'dead-lettered …')` on an ok→ok non-transition, and left S5's 'recovered' labels with no producer at all). Final contract: (A) `onStateChange(state, detail)` fires ONLY on a transition of `lastState`, via `setState` — the three producers are the retryable branch (→'retrying'), the auth branch (→'blocked'), and, newly named here, the SUCCESS path of `doShip`, which after its existing removal loop sets `blocked = false; failures = 0;` and then calls `setState('ok', \`shipped ${batch.length} item(s)\`)`. That success-path line is the producer of S5's 'Error reporting recovered' / 'Off-site backups recovered' events; it does not disturb the parity anchor because every existing ship-queue test constructs the queue without `onStateChange`, so `setState` is a no-op assignment for them. (B) `onDeadLetter(count, status)` is a SEPARATE always-fire notification, not a state signal — a dead-letter is an event, and folding it into a transition-only channel is what made the original contract unexecutable.

DEAD-LETTER CAP HAS A NAMED MECHANISM (REPAIRED per fable attack 4, which is correct: ship-queue.ts tracks no file sizes anywhere, and boot-recovery at :177-194 reads only `opts.path`, so an in-memory tally alone would reset every boot and let the file grow unbounded across restarts). Mechanism: `let deadLetterBytes: number | null = null`; on the first append, `await fs.promises.stat(`${opts.path}.deadletter.jsonl`)` inside a try/catch (ENOENT → 0) to seed the tally, then keep it in memory, adding `Buffer.byteLength(chunk)` after each successful append. Over `MAX_DEADLETTER_BYTES = 4_000_000` the append is skipped and logged once per skip — a dead-letter file is a debugging aid, not a second unbounded queue. The stat/append pair races only against another process writing the same file, which the single-server model does not do; that slack is documented in the module comment rather than defended with a lock. Dead-letter writes go through the existing `persistChain` with `fs.promises.appendFile` (never sync, never blocking a caller).

Interface additions, kept to the minimum that makes the state observable: `ShipQueue.state(): 'ok' | 'retrying' | 'blocked'` (derived: blocked → 'blocked'; failures > 0 → 'retrying'; else 'ok'), `ShipQueueOptions.onStateChange?: (state, detail: string) => void`, and `ShipQueueOptions.onDeadLetter?: (count: number, status: number) => void`. Update the module doc comment's Isolation paragraph to state the new taxonomy AND to reassert that the queue still never emits onto the Monitor bus — both callbacks are plain injected functions, exactly like `log`.
design.verification: New cases in apps/server/src/telemetry/ship-queue.test.ts, all with a transport rejecting a constructed ShipHttpError: (a) 'a 400 dead-letters the batch and keeps draining' — assert `q.size() === 0` after flush, the two items appear as two JSON lines in `<path>.deadletter.jsonl`, `onDeadLetter` called once with `(2, 400)`, `q.state() === 'ok'`, and a SECOND enqueue+flush against a now-succeeding transport ships normally; (b) 'a 401 blocks and stops rescheduling' — with fake timers, assert `q.state() === 'blocked'`, `q.size() === 1` (retained), `onStateChange` called once with 'blocked', and that advancing timers by 30 minutes produces NO further transport calls; (b2) REPAIRED ADDITION per fable attack 1 — 'a blocked queue does not ship on new enqueues': continuing from (b), `enqueue` three more items and advance fake timers by 5× flushIntervalMs, then assert the transport call count is UNCHANGED from (b), `q.size() === 4` (retention and caps still work while blocked), and the persisted JSONL on disk contains all four items; without the doShip/enqueue guards this case fails with one transport call per interval, which is precisely the defect; (c) 'flush() clears blocked and retries once' — after (b2), a succeeding transport plus `await q.flush()` empties the queue, `state() === 'ok'`, and `onStateChange` fires a second time with 'ok' (the success-path producer of S5's 'recovered' label); (c2) 'onStateChange is transition-only' — three consecutive retryable failures produce EXACTLY ONE 'retrying' emission, not three; (d) 'a 503 retains and backs off exactly as today' — the EXISTING 'retains the batch and backs off' test is duplicated with a ShipHttpError(503) and must assert the identical call counts and 60s backoff; (e) 'an unclassified rejection is still retryable' — the existing `new Error('offline')` and sync-throw tests must pass UNMODIFIED (do not touch their assertions; if either needs editing, the branch is wrong); (f) 'the dead-letter cap survives a restart' — pre-write a 4.1MB `<path>.deadletter.jsonl`, construct a fresh queue, force a 400, and assert the file was NOT appended to and a skip was logged (this is the case that fails if the tally is in-memory-only). Run `pnpm gates` and confirm the suite total is 2968 + exactly the new cases.
design.reverses: Revert ship-queue.ts and its test together; the on-disk `<path>.deadletter.jsonl` is a NEW file that pre-change code never reads or writes, so a revert leaves it as inert debris (delete it manually if desired). The `blocked` flag and the dead-letter byte tally are in-memory only — no persisted state to migrate back.

design.title: Byte-budgeted batch cut: never post a body the Worker will reject
design.intent: S3 makes a 413 survivable; this step makes it unreachable and simultaneously shrinks the poison-blast radius. Today `doShip` maps the ENTIRE store into one batch (apps/server/src/telemetry/ship-queue.ts:150-151) while the report queue retains up to `maxBytes` 2_000_000 against the Worker's MAX_BODY_BYTES of 1_000_000 — a straightforwardly reachable permanent 413. Add `ShipQueueOptions.maxBatchBytes` (default 900_000) and have `doShip` take an insertion-ordered PREFIX of `store` whose cached `lengths` sum stays within the budget, always including at least one item (a single item larger than the budget still ships alone — the Worker's own cap is then the authority, and S3 dead-letters it if it is genuinely too big). The success path already removes exactly the shipped keys, so it needs no change; only the batch construction does. Because a ship can now leave items behind, add an internal `DRAIN_DELAY_MS = 1_000`: after a SUCCESSFUL ship that leaves `store.size > 0`, reschedule at that delay instead of the full `flushIntervalMs`, so a 100-item backups backlog drains in ~100s rather than ~50 minutes. Failure paths keep the existing backoff delay untouched, and the blocked guard from S3 still outranks every reschedule site. Note the side benefit for the append-only backups queue: bundles now ship one or few at a time, so a single bad bundle takes only itself to the dead-letter file — fable attack 5 raised the resulting per-bundle request count as a cost and it SURVIVED: the outcome is intended, bounded at the queue's 100-item cap, and drained at DRAIN_DELAY_MS. Fable also probed the envelope overhead (`{"reports":[…],"dropped":N}` plus separators, unmeasured by the cached per-item lengths) and that attack likewise SURVIVED: 100_000 bytes of headroom against ~30 bytes of envelope plus one comma per item is four orders of magnitude of margin, with S3's dead-letter path as the designed backstop.
design.verification: New cases: (a) 'cuts a batch at the byte budget' — 10 items of ~200 bytes with `maxBatchBytes: 500`, assert the first transport call receives only the items that fit, in insertion order, and `q.size()` equals the remainder; (b) 'always ships at least one item' — a single item larger than `maxBatchBytes` is still passed to the transport; (c) 'drains the remainder on the short delay' — with fake timers, assert the second transport call happens at +1_000ms after a successful partial ship, not at +30_000ms; (c2) 'a blocked queue does not drain' — a partial ship followed by a 401 must produce no transport call at +1_000ms (the S3 guard must outrank DRAIN_DELAY_MS); (d) 'the dropped counter still ships with the FIRST batch and resets only on its success' — assert `dropped()` semantics are unchanged when a cut occurs (the existing drop-oldest test must pass unmodified). Run `pnpm gates`.
design.reverses: Revert ship-queue.ts to the S3 commit; `maxBatchBytes` is an optional option with a default, and no caller outside main.ts sets it, so removing it cannot break a call site.

design.title: Wire the health signal at the composition root and align the report batch cap with the Worker
design.intent: Give the operator the one signal the finding says is missing, without breaking the queue's no-emit invariant. In apps/server/src/main.ts's telemetry block (~lines 285-345): pass `maxBatchBytes: 900_000` to the reports `createShipQueue` call (explicit, with a comment naming workers/error-ingest MAX_BODY_BYTES as the number it is derived from) and leave the backups queue on the default; pass BOTH callbacks to BOTH queues, each emitting through the existing local `monitor(...)` helper as a `system` event. Mapping, now that S3 gives every label a producer: `onStateChange('blocked', d)` → label 'Error reporting blocked' | 'Off-site backups blocked'; `onStateChange('ok', d)` → label 'Error reporting recovered' | 'Off-site backups recovered' (produced by S3's success-path `setState`, and transition-only so a healthy queue emits nothing per ship); `onStateChange('retrying', d)` → label 'Error reporting retrying' | 'Off-site backups retrying' (also transition-only, so a long outage emits once, not once per attempt); `onDeadLetter(count, status)` → label 'Error reporting dead-lettered' | 'Off-site backups dead-lettered', detail `${count} item(s) after ${status} → <path>.deadletter.jsonl`. Every one of these MUST be `type: 'system'`, never `error`: an `error` event would be observed by the Reporter, enqueued, fail to ship, and re-trigger the same transition — the exact recursion the module doc warns about. This lands the signal on the Monitor bus, which is already broadcast to every connected client, so the existing in-app Monitor surfaces it with no UI work. Also extend the boot `monitor` system event to mention the dead-letter path so an operator knows where poison batches land. SEAM: this step edits the same file INIT-04-server-runtime-hardening restructures across seven of its steps (S3, S6, S10, S11, S12, S17, S18), so the two initiatives are serialized via `dependencies_on_other_initiatives` rather than left to an open question — see the metadata note there.
design.verification: No unit test exists for main.ts (server-composition-root is a 0%-coverage region — see behaviour_parity_evidence_plan). Evidence is a live-path check, recorded in the PR: run `LEDRUMS_TELEMETRY=on LEDRUMS_TELEMETRY_ENDPOINT=http://127.0.0.1:8788/ingest LEDRUMS_TELEMETRY_TOKEN=x pnpm start` against a throwaway node http stub that returns 401 for /ingest and 400 for /backups; force an error (POST a bad WS frame) and a snapshot; then confirm from the running app's Monitor panel that exactly ONE 'Error reporting blocked' system event appears (not a stream), that no further POSTs hit the stub after it EVEN WHILE new errors keep arriving (drive at least three further errors during the observation window, then read the stub's request log — this is the live-path twin of ship-queue test (b2) and the check that proves the enqueue guard is wired), that exactly ONE 'Off-site backups dead-lettered' event appears, that `<projects>/backups-outbox.jsonl.deadletter.jsonl` contains the dropped bundle, and that flipping the stub to 200 plus `await queue.flush()` on restart drains both queues and emits exactly one 'recovered' event per queue. `pnpm gates` must stay green (this step adds no tests but must not break the 2968).
design.reverses: Single-file revert of main.ts. The wiring is additive — removing `onStateChange`/`onDeadLetter`/`maxBatchBytes` leaves the queues on their defaults, which is the S4 behaviour, not the pre-initiative behaviour; a full back-out is the wave-ordered revert in rollback_strategy.

interface_deltas.note: Deliberate. The status class currently exists inside the module and is thrown away at the boundary; exporting a typed rejection is the minimum surface that lets the queue make a decision. `isRetryableStatus` is exported only so the classification has one testable home rather than being re-derived at the catch site.

A resilience initiative adds behaviour, so this cannot score on interface reduction. Four additions, one more than the pre-repair plan: one query, TWO injected callbacks (same shape as the existing `log`, preserving the no-emit invariant), one bound. The fourth is the repair for fable attack 2 — folding dead-letter notification into the transition-only `onStateChange` made the contract self-contradictory (an ok→ok emission under a transitions-only rule) and left S5's 'recovered' labels without a producer. Splitting the event channel from the state channel is the cheapest way to make both executable. Still deliberately NOT added: a `deadLettered()` counter (the callback carries the count), a `maxDeadLetterBytes` option (internal constant), an `unblock()` method (`flush()` is the escape hatch), and any per-queue policy object.

The extracted `route()` and the two size helpers stay module-internal; the Worker's public surface remains `default.fetch`. Its HTTP contract gains a 503 status but loses none. S1 does pin an implicit contract the tests rely on: `fetch` consumes exactly `req.url`, `req.method`, `req.headers` and `req.text()`.

checks: pnpm gates — full machine-locked suite; must go from 2968 green to 2968 + the new cases green, with zero pre-existing tests edited except transport.test.ts's non-2xx case (which only GAINS assertions).

The existing ship-queue.test.ts cases 'retains the batch and backs off when the transport fails, then ships on retry', 'a transport that throws never propagates out of a flush', 'drops oldest at the item cap and ships the dropped count as batch meta' and 'survives a restart' must pass BYTE-UNMODIFIED after S3 and S4 — they are the parity anchor for the retryable path, and any need to edit them is the signal that the classification branch changed transient behaviour. This still holds after the repair that adds a `setState('ok', …)` line to the success path and a `setState('retrying', …)` line to the failure path: every one of those tests constructs the queue WITHOUT `onStateChange`, so `setState` reduces to a local assignment with no observable effect. If any of them goes red, the added lines did more than record state.
New ship-queue case (d) in S3 duplicates the backoff test against ShipHttpError(503) and asserts the identical transport call counts and the identical 60s second-attempt timing.

New ship-queue case (b2) in S3 is the anti-treadmill regression test: enqueue while blocked and assert zero additional transport calls across 5 flush intervals. Without it the suite cannot distinguish a queue that stopped shipping from one that merely reports 'blocked' while POSTing rejected credentials every 30s.

New ship-queue case (f) in S3 is the dead-letter cap regression test: a pre-existing over-cap file must be respected by a freshly constructed queue, proving the tally is seeded by a stat rather than assumed zero at boot.
The 4 existing workers/error-ingest/test/index.test.ts auth/404/invalid-JSON cases must pass unmodified after S1, proving the route extraction moved no routing behaviour.
pnpm typecheck across the workspace (workers/* is a pnpm workspace member, so the Worker is type-gated by `pnpm gates` too).

Manual live-path script (S5 verification): a throwaway node http stub returning programmable statuses (200/401/400/413/503) with a request log, driven against a real `pnpm start` server; assert the Monitor event sequence, the stub's request log AFTER further errors are driven post-block, and the contents of `error-reports.jsonl`, `backups-outbox.jsonl` and their `.deadletter.jsonl` siblings after each status.
behaviour_parity_evidence_plan.known_gaps: A green suite cannot prove parity for three regions here. (1) apps/server/src/main.ts is a 0%-coverage composition root (server lane is 72.31% lines overall, and the telemetry wiring block has no test at all) — S5 is entirely inside it. The replacing evidence is the scripted stub-server live-path run above: it exercises the actual wired queues, the actual Monitor bus and the actual on-disk outboxes, and its Monitor output plus stub request log are pasted into the PR as the artefact. (2) Nothing in CI ever speaks HTTP to the real Worker — there is no miniflare/wrangler test harness, and D1/R2 are faked at the store seam, so the 503 boundary is proven only against a fake Env whose binding throws. The replacing evidence is a `npx wrangler@4 dev --local` smoke with the D1 binding pointed at a non-existent database, curl'ing /ingest and /reports and capturing the actual 503 JSON body; plus a post-deploy curl against the live Worker for the same two routes. Note that S1's repaired verification (c) uses a hand-built Request-like object rather than a real `Request` (undici recomputes content-length on a real Request with a body), so the fast-reject path is proven against the four members `fetch` actually touches, not against a real runtime Request — the wrangler smoke with a genuine oversized POST is what closes that gap. (3) Timing behaviour is proven with vitest fake timers, not real clocks, so the drain cadence (S4's DRAIN_DELAY_MS) and the 30-minute backoff ceiling are asserted structurally rather than observed; the stub-server run covers the drain cadence in real time for a small backlog only, and the 30-minute ceiling remains unobserved by design (nobody will sit through it). Claiming 'none' anywhere here would be false.
behaviour_parity_evidence_plan.baseline_reference: Phase 0 baseline sha 3708648, 2968 tests green under `pnpm gates`; coverage baseline docs/plans/2026-07-26-deep-review/00-coverage.json (server 72.31% lines). Plan assumes fix batches 1-3 (dead-code auto-fixes, dead-code residue, kit-mirror removal) have already landed on top of it; none of those touch apps/server/src/telemetry or workers/error-ingest, so the baseline is unmoved for this initiative's files. It further assumes INIT-04-server-runtime-hardening has landed (see dependencies_on_other_initiatives), which moves apps/server/src/main.ts but does not extract its telemetry block — S5 is therefore written against the same block either way, only at shifted line numbers.

rollback_strategy: Five commits across four waves, each independently revertable in reverse order (S5 → S4 → S3 → S2 → S1). There is no data migration and no schema change; the only new persistent artefact is `<queue path>.deadletter.jsonl`, which pre-change code neither reads nor writes, so reverting leaves it as inert debris rather than corrupting the outbox. The `blocked` state and the dead-letter byte tally are in-memory only, so a revert plus a process restart restores the exact pre-initiative retain-and-backoff behaviour on the next boot. Two ordering constraints: (a) S3 without S2 does not compile (it consumes ShipHttpError), so reverting S2 alone is invalid — revert the pair; (b) the Worker is a SEPARATE deploy unit — reverting S1 in git does nothing to the live Worker until `pnpm --filter @ledrums/error-ingest-worker deploy` is re-run from the reverted tree, and the client-side classification (S2-S5) is safe against BOTH Worker versions because the old Worker's bare 500 is a 5xx and therefore classified retryable, i.e. today's behaviour. Partial rollback is therefore safe in either direction. One behaviour to know before reverting S3 in isolation: a queue that has entered `blocked` in the running process stays blocked until `flush()` or a restart, so a revert-and-redeploy must include a process restart to guarantee the old retry loop resumes. Fastest kill switch without any revert: unset LEDRUMS_TELEMETRY_ENDPOINT / set LEDRUMS_TELEMETRY=off, which disables both queues entirely and leaves capture feeding the local Monitor.

open_questions.question: Should a blocked/dead-lettering queue get a visible badge in the app (BackupsDialog or TopBar), or is the Monitor `system` event the whole signal? This plan chose the Monitor event alone — a badge means a design-system extension plus a `pnpm ui-shot` pass, which is real UI work this initiative would otherwise not touch.

The report queue retains up to maxBytes 2_000_000 while the Worker caps a body at MAX_BODY_BYTES 1_000_000. This plan fixes the mismatch on the CLIENT (batch cut at 900_000). Should the Worker's cap instead rise to 2MB+ so a full queue always ships in one request?

On a persistent 401 (rotated TELEMETRY_TOKEN), should the backups queue keep accepting snapshots until it silently drop-oldests at its 100-item cap, or should `enqueue` hard-stop while blocked so nothing is written that will certainly be lost? This plan keeps accepting (drops are counted and reported on recovery), which favours a token fix arriving soon — and the S3 repair makes the choice sharper, since a blocked queue now accumulates without ever attempting a ship.

Is a dead-lettered batch expected to be recoverable — i.e. should a later step re-ingest `<path>.deadletter.jsonl` after a schema fix — or is it purely a forensic artefact? This plan treats it as forensic (capped at 4MB, never re-read), which is the smaller design.

Ordering with INIT-04-server-runtime-hardening is now a hard edge in dependencies_on_other_initiatives (INIT-04 lands first) rather than a non-blocking note, because S5 and seven INIT-04 steps mutate apps/server/src/main.ts and the seam gate is constitutional. The schema's field only expresses 'must land before', and INIT-04 was chosen as the earlier side because it is the far larger main.ts churn while S5 is a ~15-line additive edit inside a block INIT-04 does not extract. Confirm that direction, or invert it if INIT-11 is wanted sooner — the constraint that must not be relaxed either way is that the two never run concurrently.

The `blocked` flag is in-memory, and boot-recovery schedules a flush on construction, so every process restart spends exactly one rejected POST re-testing a rotated token before blocking again. Is one 401 per boot the right cost for automatic recovery after a credential fix, or should the blocked state persist alongside the JSONL so a restart stays quiet until an operator acts?

Should `blocked` auto-clear after a long cooldown (say 1 hour) so a queue recovers without operator action, or is `flush()` plus a restart the only intended exit? This plan chose no cooldown — an auto-retry ladder on top of a permanent-failure state re-introduces a slower version of the treadmill the initiative exists to remove — but a headless deployment with nobody watching the Monitor may want one.

attacks_addressed: S3: the 'blocked' state does not actually stop shipping — enqueue re-arms the flush timer unconditionally (ship-queue.ts:206) and doShip has no state guard, so a live error stream keeps POSTing one rejected request per interval while state() reports 'blocked'.

S3/S5: the onStateChange contract is self-contradictory (transitions-only, yet branch (3) emits an ok→ok dead-letter notification) and leaves S5's 'recovered' labels with no producer at all, since the success path was declared byte-unchanged.
S1: verification (c)'s DB.prepare-spy assertion is vacuous — DB access is already unreachable on today's 413 path, so the test passes against an implementation that buffers the whole body first.
S3: MAX_DEADLETTER_BYTES is unimplementable across restarts — no mechanism is named for knowing the current file size, and an in-memory tally resets every boot.
Metadata: the INIT-04 mutation seam on apps/server/src/main.ts was declared only as a non-blocking open question while dependencies_on_other_initiatives — the field the scheduler reads — said [].
S4 (survived): the 900_000 default also applies to the backups queue, degrading it to one bundle per request against a 16MB route cap.
S2 (survived): deploy skew, where S2-S5 land against a pre-S1 Worker whose faults are bare 500s.
S4 (survived): the byte budget measures cached per-item lengths, not the posted body with its envelope and separators.
synthesis_inputs.rationale:
DISCLOSURE, read this first: this is a REPAIRED OPUS PLAN, not a merge of two rival designs. INIT-11 ran on the light track, which produced exactly one plan variant (07-plans/INIT-11-telemetry-resilience/opus.json). Fable is listed in variants_considered only to satisfy the schema's minItems 2; fable's actual contribution is the refutation artifact (08-refutations/INIT-11-telemetry-resilience.fable.json, verdict 'sound-with-repairs', rubric correctness 3 / parity 4 / sequencing 3 / blast-radius 4 / verification 4), never a competing plan. Nothing was chosen between designs, because there was only one design.

WHAT SURVIVED UNCHANGED: the entire structural shape — the four-concept design (Worker 503 fault boundary, typed ShipHttpError, queue outcome policy, byte-budgeted batch cut), the five steps and their four waves, the refusal to classify retries inside the Worker, the refusal of a bespoke backups-health UI panel, the refusal of an outbox rewrite, the no-emit isolation invariant with the composition root owning Monitor emission, the `system`-never-`error` rule that prevents recursion, the retain-and-backoff parity anchor for the retryable path, the rollback ordering, and the deploy-skew safety argument. Three of fable's eight attacks landed on the plan's side and forced no change: per-bundle backups shipping (S4 names it as intended and it is bounded by the 100-item cap and DRAIN_DELAY_MS), deploy skew (isRetryableStatus(500) is true, so a pre-S1 Worker behaves exactly as today), and envelope overhead versus the byte budget (100KB of headroom against ~30 bytes plus one comma per item, with the dead-letter path as backstop).

REPAIRS FORCED BY SURVIVING ATTACKS — all five of fable's required_repairs applied, each spot-checked against source rather than taken on trust:
(1) The blocked state now actually blocks — fable attack 1, major, and the most serious defect in the plan. Verified against source: ship-queue.ts:197-207 shows `enqueue` calling `scheduleFlush(flushIntervalMs)` unconditionally as its last act, and doShip at :147-175 has no state guard of any kind; main.ts:296-301 confirms the reports queue is keyed by dedupKey and upserted continuously. So the original 'tick/flush must check blocked before calling scheduleFlush' would have produced a queue that reports 'blocked' to the operator while POSTing rejected credentials once per flush interval forever. S3 now gates at THREE sites — `doShip(force = false)` returns early when blocked (the authoritative guard), `enqueue` skips its scheduleFlush while blocked but keeps keying/capping/persisting, and every reschedule site checks blocked — with `flush()` passing force:true as the operator escape hatch. New test (b2) enqueues after the block and asserts zero further transport calls across five intervals, and S5's live-path check now drives further errors post-block and reads the stub's request log, which is the live twin of the same property.

(2) The state-change contract is now executable and every label has a producer — fable attack 2, major. The original said onStateChange fires 'only on a TRANSITION' and then emitted onStateChange('ok', 'dead-lettered…') on a first-attempt 400, which is ok→ok and therefore forbidden by its own rule; symmetrically it left S5's 'recovered' labels with no producer because blocked→ok happens in the success path, which the parity anchor declared byte-unchanged. Repair: split the channels. `onStateChange` fires only through an internal `setState(next, detail)` that compares against `lastState`, with three named producers — the retryable branch, the auth branch, and (newly named) the success path of doShip, which sets `blocked = false; failures = 0;` and then emits 'ok'. `onDeadLetter(count, status)` is a separate always-fire event channel. This costs a fourth interface addition, recorded honestly in interface_deltas. The parity anchor survives because every existing ship-queue test constructs the queue without callbacks, so setState is a local assignment for them — that reasoning is written into behaviour_parity_evidence_plan checks[1] as the falsifiable form: if those tests go red, the added lines did more than record state.

(3) S1 verification (c) now tests the property it claims — fable attack 3, minor but correct. Verified against index.ts:39-41 and :54-63: on today's 413 path the body is read first and DB access is already unreachable, so the DB.prepare spy is vacuously un-called before and after the change. Replaced with a spy on body consumption. The replacement is executable because S1's intent pins the exact request surface `fetch` uses — I confirmed from source that it touches only `req.url` (line 34), `req.method`/`url.pathname` (39, 68, 74, 93, 99), `req.headers.get('authorization')` (27) and `req.text()` (40, 76) — so a hand-built `{ method, url, headers: new Headers(...), text: vi.fn() } as unknown as Request` is a faithful stand-in, and a real `Request` would be the wrong tool here because undici recomputes content-length from the body. The residual gap (this is not a runtime Request) is now stated in known_gaps and closed by the wrangler smoke.

(4) The dead-letter cap has a named mechanism that survives restarts — fable attack 4, minor but correct. Verified: ship-queue.ts tracks no file sizes anywhere, and boot-recovery at :177-194 reads only opts.path, never a dead-letter sibling. S3 now specifies a lazy `fs.promises.stat` on first append (ENOENT → 0) seeding an in-memory tally maintained by adding each appended chunk's byte length, with the single-writer race documented as accepted slack rather than defended with a lock. New test (f) pre-writes an over-cap file, constructs a fresh queue, and asserts no append — the case that fails if the tally is assumed zero at boot.

(5) The INIT-04 seam is now a machine-readable edge — fable attack 5, major, and correct on the constitutional point: the seam gate is not something a scheduler can read out of prose. Verified against 09-synthesis/INIT-04-server-runtime-hardening.json: seven of its nineteen steps (S3, S6, S10, S11, S12, S17, S18) list apps/server/src/main.ts, and its own dependencies array is [], so nothing prevented a concurrent dispatch. `dependencies_on_other_initiatives` is now ['INIT-04-server-runtime-hardening']. The schema's field expresses only 'must land before', so a direction had to be chosen: INIT-04 first, because it is by far the larger main.ts churn while S5 is a ~15-line additive edit — and crucially INIT-04 does NOT extract the telemetry block (its main.ts steps extract ws-broadcast, ws-connection, stats-frame and persisted-slot), so S5 is written against the same block either way, only at shifted line numbers. That fact also retires the original open question's second half ('should S5 be written against INIT-04's extracted telemetry module') — there is no such module. The open question that remains asks Trent only to confirm or invert the direction, with the never-concurrent constraint held either way.

OTHER CHANGES: estimated_loc raised 330 → 380 for the third blocked guard, the setState helper, the fourth callback and the four added test cases. Two new open questions surfaced BY the repairs rather than by fable — whether the in-memory blocked flag should persist (a restart now spends exactly one rejected POST re-testing a rotated token, which is the price of automatic recovery) and whether blocked should auto-clear on a cooldown for headless deployments — both owner trent, both non-blocking, both consequences of making the block real that did not exist while the block was leaky.
